Jersey City: Total energy and pneumatic trash collection systems are planned for this site. The total energy system contributes to improved air quality and economy by reducing fuel consumption for a required energy demand. The total energy plant will generate electric power for all normal site loads, and will use the exhaust heat to provide domestic hot water, inside heating and air conditioning. The use of total energy systems in residential and commercial installations is not new; about thirty such systems are now in operation in residential developments. However, no provision has been made to adequately record and report the operating costs and parameters for these plants, and the installation at Jersey City is intended to fill this gap. HUD and NBS will be documenting first costs, operating costs, energy flow and reliability, in order to develop the basic information necessary for consideration of total energy installations as an alternative energy supply. HUD will lease the installation from the site developer as a National Test Facility.
Also in Jersey City, a Swedish-developed pneumatic trash collection system will be demonstrated and tested. In this system, refuse is gathered through sealed vacuum tubing directly from the disposal chute to a central collecting and compacting location with no intermediate handling. This system is expected to reduce the refuse volume, and to prevent overflowing dustbins, smells, dust, noise and spillage during loading and transport. It also will reduce the number of truck access locations otherwise required.
Specific attention is being given to the design of the Central Equipment Building and to selection of the equipment to minimize the acoustical radiation from these facilities.
Finally, the New Jersey Bell Telephone Company will have a telephone supermarket at the Jersey City site. This will allow residents to select the telephone equipment they desire and plug it into pre-installed jacks located throughout each apartment. The residents benefit from instant service and the telephone company does not have to send installers out on costly assignments.
Indianapolis: Precipitation history and the very flat gradient of the Indianapolis site document a history of flooding under heavy spring and summer rains in this area. The site planner, both to provide a more attractive visual environment and to reduce the downstream flooding impact of this site, developed an earthmoving program which created holding basins in the open space areas of the site to reduce the instantaneous volume of storm water flow. This program has also resulted in a smaller and less expensive storm drainage system. The site planners and the Indiana State Division of Water Resources are studying the effectiveness of this design approach.
